summary: A target-level continuation of the Tau Ceti ModularForms roadmap, covering the noncongruence arithmetic of Calegari–Dimitrov–Tang and its stated applications. It imports the weakly holomorphic carrier from QSeriesPartitionsAndMockModularForms, the cohomological Ihara inputs from ModularCurvesPartII R14.4, the arithmetic holonomy bound from DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendencePartII and the uniformization of ℂ∖μ_N from ConformalMappingPartII. Five exact gaps remain (MODEL, NF, GLOCAL, LOCALGLOBAL, NERON). No target is claimed implemented.

nodes.title: Weak forms on finite-index subgroups: the cusp-germ characterization
nodes.statement: Let Γ≤SL₂(ℤ) have finite index, regarded in GL₂(ℝ) through the existing coercion, and let k∈ℤ. The space M^!_k(Γ) of weakly holomorphic modular forms is imported from QSeriesPartitionsAndMockModularForms:QM.3/weakly-holomorphic-modular-form: functions holomorphic on ℍ, invariant under the weight-k slash action of Γ, with exponential growth at every cusp. A function f:ℍ→ℂ lies in M^!_k(Γ) if and only if it is holomorphic on ℍ, Γ-invariant, and for every g∈SL₂(ℤ) the slash f|ₖg is periodic with some positive strict period h and its cusp function in q_h is meromorphic at q_h=0, so that its Laurent series has finite principal part. The elements with no negative Laurent term at any cusp are exactly the existing ModularForm Γ k. M^!_k(Γ) is preserved by restriction to a finite-index subgroup, and products add weights. In this roadmap a weak form is an element of M^!_k(Γ) for a finite-index Γ≤SL₂(ℤ), and a weak modular function is the case k=0. Character-valued forms keep the parent character carrier and are not folded into this trivial-character space.
proofSteps: For g∈SL₂(ℤ), f|ₖg is weakly holomorphic for the finite-index conjugate g⁻¹Γg, which is arithmetic with determinant one. Apply the imported Laurent-expansion theorem QM.3/weakly-holomorphic-laurent-expansion at its cusp ∞: exponential growth there is equivalent to a Laurent series with finite principal part, that is, to meromorphy of the cusp function at q_h=0.

Every rational cusp is g∞ for some g∈SL₂(ℤ), so the condition for all g is exponential growth at every cusp. Changing g inside its coset of the cusp stabilizer, or replacing h by a positive multiple, changes the Laurent variable by a root of unity or a power and preserves the condition. Nonnegative Laurent support at every cusp is boundedness at every cusp (FuchsianOrbifolds Layer 3, item 5), the existing ModularForm condition.

A cusp of a finite-index subgroup is a cusp of Γ, and growth at a cusp does not depend on the group, which gives restriction. For determinant-one matrices the slash of a product is the product of the slashes, and principal parts multiply.
acceptance: The constant 1 lies in M^!_0(SL₂(ℤ)); Δ⁻¹ lies in M^!_{−12}(SL₂(ℤ)), its expansion begins with Q⁻¹, and it is not an existing ModularForm.
For a∈ℂ, (j−a)⁻¹ is rejected because j−a has a zero on ℍ: weak forms have no interior poles; a pole at a rational cusp is allowed.
Changing the scaling matrix or replacing a strict period by a positive multiple preserves the cusp-germ condition.

nodes.title: Bounded denominators of a Fourier germ
nodes.statement: For an embedded number field K⊆ℂ and a Laurent series a(t)∈K((t)), bounded denominators means there is one nonzero d∈O_K with d a_n∈O_K for every coefficient, including the finite principal part. Over ℚ use one integer D≥1. This is scalar denominator clearing, not substitution t↦t/M. For a holomorphic germ f with positive strict period 2N, its Taylor series is UpperHalfPlane.qExpansion (2N) f in t=e^{πiτ/N}. Integral coefficients mean every coefficient lies in the embedded ℤ, or O_K, as appropriate.
proofSteps: Use coefficientwise membership in the image of O_K and quantify a single clearing scalar.
Addition and convolution preserve a common clearing scalar after multiplying denominators; finite Laurent support below zero permits the same argument.
acceptance: Never infer bounded denominators from membership in O_K[1/S][[t]].
State the period separately: existence of Taylor coefficients alone does not identify a Fourier germ.

sources.match: The arithmetic condition is one scalar clearing all Fourier coefficients. The number-field remarks use algebraic integers; this does not follow just from allowing a finite set of denominator primes.

nodes.title: Geometric Wohlfahrt level
nodes.statement: Write E={±I}, Γᵖ=⟨Γ,E⟩. At g∞ define the signed width wᵍ(Γ) to be the least m>0 with either gT^m g⁻¹ or −gT^m g⁻¹ in Γ. Define L(Γ) as the lcm over the finitely many Γᵖ-cusps of these widths. This equals L(Γᵖ). For E≤Γ, signed width agrees with the existing integerCuspWidth of the conjugate group. Without E≤Γ a strict width may be twice a signed width; odd weights then retain the associated sign in the local parameter.
proofSteps: Import cusp representatives and the strict translation subgroup from FuchsianOrbifolds. Pass to the projective closure before taking the lcm.
Prove representative independence using the signed stabilizer and positive generator of its translation image.
acceptance: This level is geometric; it does not mean the subgroup is congruence.
Level is positive for finite-index groups and is unchanged by adjoining −I.

sources.match: The level is the common multiple of geometric cusp ramification orders. Passing to the projective closure makes the sign convention explicit and distinguishes this from a strict translation width.

nodes.title: Clearing cusp poles with Δ
nodes.statement: For f weak of weight k on finite-index Γ, there exists m≥0 such that fΔ^m is an existing holomorphic ModularForm Γ (k+12m). Multiplication by Δ^m is injective, since Δ has no zero on ℍ. At each cusp the order of Δ is positive. This statement includes irregular cusps and does not assume −I∈Γ.
proofSteps: There are finitely many cusps. For each choose m to offset the finite negative Laurent order using the positive local order of Δ.
Take the maximum; retain the slash multiplier in an irregular cusp chart and compare boundedness with ModularForm.
acceptance: Δ⁻¹ becomes the constant 1 after one multiplication.
The construction preserves all interior holomorphy conditions.

sources.match: The containment argument multiplies a weak modular function by a sufficiently large power of the discriminant. Its positive order at every cusp and absence of zeros on the upper half-plane justify this reduction.

nodes.title: Level of an intersection
nodes.statement: If E≤G,H and both have finite index, the signed cusp width of G∩H at each rational cusp is lcm(w(G),w(H)); consequently L(G∩H)=lcm(L(G),L(H)). In particular L(G),L(H)∣N implies L(G∩H)∣N.
proofSteps: With E included, membership of a translation in both stabilizers is exactly divisibility by both positive generators.
Take the lcm over a common refinement of cusp representatives.
acceptance: Do not apply the unsigned equality to two groups that exclude −I.

sources.match: The intersection lemma computes geometric level after intersecting subgroups. The target retains the central sign hypothesis needed for equality of cusp stabilizer translation subgroups.

nodes.title: Geometric level of the normal core
nodes.statement: For finite-index G≤SL₂(ℤ) containing E, the existing ambient normal core G.normalCore has finite index, contains E, and has exactly L(G).
proofSteps: The coset action has finite image, so the core is an intersection of finitely many conjugates.
Each conjugate has the same level; combine the intersection formula with core≤G.
acceptance: Taking a core cannot silently erase the E hypothesis.

sources.match: The core lemma retains geometric level under the finite intersection of conjugates. Finite index turns the ambient normal core into that finite intersection.

nodes.title: Level after p-scaling
nodes.statement: Let H contain E, have finite index and L(H)=N. For p prime, A=diag(p,1), set Hᴀ=A⁻¹HA∩SL₂(ℤ). Then Hᴀ has finite index, contains E and L(Hᴀ)∣Np. A does not lie in SL₂(ℤ); conjugation is performed in GL₂(ℚ) before intersection.
proofSteps: Represent a cusp by a primitive integer column and split according to divisibility of its entries by p.
Compute the conjugated parabolic explicitly in each case. In the second case the correcting diagonal is diag(1/p,p); the final translation exponent is Np.
acceptance: A cusp with a p-divisible primitive coordinate exercises the corrected second case.

sources.match: The scaling lemma bounds the new geometric level by the old level times p. The target corrects the diagonal in the second primitive-column case and performs conjugation in rational matrices.

nodes.title: Wohlfahrt’s theorem with signs
nodes.statement: If a finite-index congruence G contains E, then Γ(L(G))≤G. For an arbitrary congruence G, the conclusion is Γ(L(G))≤⟨G,E⟩. Thus a congruence subgroup containing E and with geometric level dividing N contains Γ(N).
proofSteps: Apply KSV10 Proposition 3 and Remark 8 with the translations gT^N g⁻¹ available because E≤G. First modify a matrix of Γ(N) by elementary N-transvections so its lower-right entry is coprime to an existing congruence level ν. CRT avoiding one residue for each prime dividing ν suffices in place of Dirichlet.

Clear the off-diagonal entries modulo ν. In KSV10 equation (1) use M=(T^(1−d))ᵗ L T^(d−1), L=[[a,a−1],[1−a,2−a]]. Its correct further factorization is L=(Tᵗ)⁻¹ T^(a−1) Tᵗ; the displayed line on p.6 reverses these conjugating signs. Reduction leaves an element of Γ(ν)≤G. Adjoin E for the general case.
acceptance: H′ at level 2 gives a counterexample to removing E from the first conclusion.

sources.match: The nonabelian Ihara proof invokes Wohlfahrt to turn geometric level into a principal subgroup inclusion. KSV10 supplies the primary elementary proof; adjoining the central sign is essential to the stated general version.

nodes.title: The modular λ function
nodes.statement: Using the pinned η on ℂ, set x(τ)=(η(τ/2)η(2τ)²/η(τ)³)^8 and λ(τ)=16x(τ). On ℍ the denominator is nonzero. Pin q=e^{πiτ}: x=q∏_{n≥1}((1+q^{2n})/(1+q^{2n−1}))^8. The associated formal series is the integral q-adic product; agreement with the analytic product is a theorem, not a choice of a formal expansion. Its λ-normalization sends the three Γ(2)-cusps ∞,0,1 to 0,1,∞.
proofSteps: Build the analytic function from the existing η and prove its product identity by separating even and odd factors.
Use the imported theta/eta identities to obtain λ=(θ₂/θ₃)^4, the S and T transformations, and its cusp limits.
acceptance: The analytic λ is holomorphic and avoids 0 and 1 on ℍ.
The coefficient of q in λ is 16; the integral coordinate x has coefficient 1.

sources.match: The eta product defines the coordinate with leading term 16q. Its theta expression, integral normalization and cusp values fix which of the six usual lambda normalizations is used.

nodes.title: The λ covering and three cusp values
nodes.statement: λ:ℍ→ℂ∖{0,1} is a holomorphic universal covering with effective deck group Γ(2)/E. It extends to a biholomorphism X(2)≃ℙ¹ sending ∞,0,1 to 0,1,∞. For every finite-index H≤Γ(2) containing E, Y(H)→Y(2) is finite unramified, and the compactified map is branched only above these three values; finite covers are read using the imported covering correspondence.
proofSteps: Show λ separates the Γ(2) fundamental domain using theta transformations, cusp values and reflection.
Use the degree-one meromorphic map X(2)→ℙ¹ and the imported degree theorem. Identify deck transformations projectively and use universal-cover lifting.
acceptance: −I acts trivially, so Γ(2) itself is not the effective deck group.
Disc lifts used in W3 are holomorphic on Y(H).

sources.match: The modular pullback uses lambda as the universal covering of the twice-punctured plane. The target derives the compactified degree-one coordinate from the imported quotient and covering geometry.

nodes.title: The level-two modular-function ring
nodes.statement: The ring of complex weight-zero weak forms on Γ(2) is ℂ[λ,λ⁻¹,(1−λ)⁻¹]. Its subring with rational Fourier coefficients at ∞ is ℚ[λ,λ⁻¹,(1−λ)⁻¹]; its fraction field is ℚ(λ). A rational q expansion forces a rational function in λ to have rational coefficients by the integral inverse coordinate and uniqueness of a reduced rational function.
proofSteps: On ℙ¹ a function with poles only at 0,1,∞ is a rational function in the coordinate with precisely these allowed denominators.
Apply the rational germ criterion at 0 to descend constants from ℂ to ℚ.
acceptance: λ⁻¹ and (1−λ)⁻¹ are required; ℚ[λ] alone misses cusp poles.

sources.match: The field definition uses rational functions of lambda as scalars. Identifying the compactification with the projective line gives the allowed pole ring, and the rational Fourier germ descends its coefficients.

nodes.title: Integral λ reparametrization
nodes.statement: The formal x(q)=λ(q)/16 has a unique compositional inverse q(x) in x+x²ℤ[[x]]. Substitution gives mutually inverse ℤ-algebra maps ℤ[[q]]≃ℤ[[x]], and similarly over ℚ and any coefficient ring obtained by scalar extension. Its first terms are q=x+8x²+84x³+992x⁴+12514x⁵ modulo x⁶.
proofSteps: The linear term is the unit 1. Solve successively for the coefficient of the inverse without division by any nonunit.
Pass from truncated inverse identities to equality of power series and to analytic germs in a small disc.
acceptance: Compute compositions through degree five in both orders.
This asserts a formal change of variable, not an equality of two independently named formal indeterminates.

sources.match: The argument changes from q to lambda/16 without introducing denominators, because the normalized series has linear coefficient one. The target includes the inverse coefficients and two-sided substitution identities.

nodes.title: The normalized Kummer coordinate
nodes.statement: For N≥1 and t=q^{1/N}, there is a unique x_N(t)∈t+t²ℚ[[t]] with x_N(t)^N=x(t^N). It belongs to t+t²ℤ[1/N][[t]], and x_N^N is integral. Branches are fixed by x_N/t→1. No claim is made that x_N itself is integral for arbitrary N. Pulling back x=λ/16 by u↦u^N leaves possible singularities at 16^{−1/N}μ_N and ∞; width dividing 2N removes monodromy at u=0.
proofSteps: Write x(t^N)=t^N times an integral unit with constant term 1 and solve for its normalized N-th root over ℤ[1/N].
Use the cusp local monodromy order bound to remove the apparent singularity at zero after this pullback.
acceptance: N=1 recovers x.
For N=3, x_N=t−(8/3)t⁴+⋯, so general integral-root claims fail.

sources.match: The holonomy embedding takes a normalized N-th root of lambda/16. The proof needs its N-th power integral, and does not require the root itself to have integral coefficients.

nodes.title: Jacobi’s hypergeometric identity with character
nodes.statement: Let K₀(x)=Σ_{n≥0}binom(2n,n)²x^n = ₂F₁(1/2,1/2;1;16x). Then K₀(x(τ))=θ₃(τ)². This is weight 1 on Γ(2) with χ(γ)=χ_{−4}(dγ), and is a trivial-character form on H′={γ∈Γ(2):dγ≡1 mod4}. The series is integral and transcendental over ℚ(x); its equation x(1−16x)y″+(1−32x)y′−4y=0 has nontrivial unipotent local monodromy at 0, despite this particular holomorphic branch.
proofSteps: Compare the normalized analytic solution of the hypergeometric equation with the theta product.
Square the imported theta transformation, retaining χ_{−4}(d). Obtain logarithmic continuation at 0 from the second independent solution to prove infinite monodromy.
acceptance: Constant coefficient 1 excludes the zero solution.
−I acts by −1 in weight 1; a trivial Γ(2) character would contradict parity.

sources.locator: Equations (1.1.4)–(1.1.5), p.631; Remark 7.2.3 and (7.2.4), p.688; corrected character in extraction E12
sources.match: The Jacobi identity identifies the integral hypergeometric series with theta-three squared. The target restores its weight-one character and keeps the infinite unipotent monodromy that prevents the algebraicity theorem from applying.

nodes.title: Two modular uniformization checks
nodes.statement: With C(z)=i(1−z)/(1+z), F₂(z)=2λ(C(z))−1 universally covers ℂ∖{±1}, sends 0 to 0, and |F₂′(0)|=Γ(1/4)^4/(4π²)>4. The supplier’s N=3 normalized covering has |F₃′(0)|=Γ(1/6)^3/(12π^{3/2})>16^{1/3}; its η-quotient in Example 5.1.22 agrees with that covering after the chosen rotation. Among N≥2, ℂ∖μ_N is isomorphic to Y(N) only for N=2,3.
proofSteps: Compose the λ covering with the Cayley transform and the affine map u↦2u−1; F₂ is a pointed universal covering of ℂ∖{±1}.

Specialize ConformalMappingPartII:R0/conformal-radius-formula at N=2 and N=3; for N=2 the pointed cover is unique up to rotation (ConformalMappingPartII:U0/roots-cover), so |F₂′(0)| is the stated Gamma value. Match the η-quotient of CDT Example 5.1.22 at N=3 with the normalized cover by its value and derivative at 0.

For the last assertion compare punctures and genus: ℂ∖μ_N is the sphere minus N+1 points, Y(2) and Y(3) are spheres minus 3 and 4 points with the matching cross-ratio, Y(4) and Y(5) have 6 and 12 cusps, and Y(N) has positive genus for N≥6.
acceptance: F₂(0)=0 and its target omits exactly ±1.
The N=2 derivative is about 4.37687923 and the N=3 derivative about 2.5810565.

sources.match: The example evaluates the N=2 and N=3 covering radii using gamma values and eta quotients. These are acceptance cases for the imported punctured-plane theorem, not a new general uniformization theory.

nodes.title: The field M₂N
nodes.statement: For N≥1 take t=q^{1/N}, x=λ/16 and the common ambient Laurent field ℚ((t)). M₂N is the ℚ(λ)-linear span of q expansions of weight-zero weak forms on ⟨E,Γ(2N)⟩ with rational coefficients at ∞. Each generating function is holomorphic on Y(2N); poles at cusps are permitted. The embedded ℚ(λ) is specified by the λ series. Its field structure is proved below rather than included as an axiom.
proofSteps: Map actual analytic functions to their Laurent expansions, using injectivity of the expansion germ.
Form the linear span over the explicitly embedded rational-function field.
acceptance: For N=1, M₂=ℚ(λ).
No arbitrary complex constants enter the rational coefficient field.

sources.match: The first field is defined as a rational-function span of rational weak modular functions at principal level. Field structure is a subsequent result, rather than part of an unverified definition.

nodes.title: The field R₂N
nodes.statement: Inside the same ℚ((q^{1/N})), R₂N is the ℚ(λ)-linear span of expansions at ∞ of rational-coefficient weight-zero weak forms invariant under some finite-index group H containing E with every cusp width dividing 2N, and having one common denominator. Equivalently choose an admissible H for each generator. A generator can have finitely many negative terms; multiplication by a power of λ makes it holomorphic at ∞ without changing the span. The ℚ(λ)-span itself can introduce interior poles through rational functions of λ.
proofSteps: Use the union of admissible generating sets, not a fixed group asserted in advance.
Separate holomorphic generators from the scalar span so that field division does not impose false interior holomorphy.
acceptance: The admissible group is existential and can vary with the generator.
A fixed finite denominator is required.

sources.match: The second span permits finite-index stabilizers with bounded geometric level and bounded rational Fourier denominators. The target specifies the ambient Laurent field and distinguishes its generators from arbitrary scalar combinations.

nodes.title: Congruence functions have bounded denominators
nodes.statement: For all N≥1, M₂N⊆R₂N as subspaces in the specified Laurent field.
proofSteps: Apply the exact all-prime bounded-denominator supplier to fΔ^m, not just a lattice over ℤ[1/(2N)].
Divide by the integral unit-times-monomial expansion Δ^m=q^{2m}∏(1−q^{2n})^{24m}; principal level gives every width dividing 2N.
acceptance: The primes dividing 2N are included in the denominator conclusion.

sources.match: The inclusion uses the congruence bounded-denominator theorem after clearing cusp poles by the discriminant. It needs a bound at every prime, including primes dividing the level.

nodes.title: The modular holonomy embedding
nodes.statement: For N≥1 let U_N=ℂ∖16^{−1/N}μ_N, t=q^{1/N}, let χ=x_N(t) be the normalized Kummer coordinate of W2/kummer-coordinate and p(u)=u^N, so that p(χ(t))=x(t^N)=λ/16 is integral and ℚ(p)=ℚ(λ). Read through the formal inverse of χ, every element of R₂N lies in the ℚ(p)-span W(U_N,χ,p) of the integral holonomic ring H(U_N,χ,ℤ) of DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendencePartII:AA.4. Each generator enters H after multiplication by a nonzero integer clearing its denominators and by a power of p clearing its pole at ∞; general elements are ℚ(λ)-combinations of these. The containment is in W and not only in the larger ℚ(u)-span V, because χ is not integral for N≥2.
proofSteps: A generator f of R₂N is invariant under a finite-index H containing E with cusp widths dividing 2N, so it is a rational function on the algebraic curve Y(H), finite étale over Y(2) (W2/lambda-covering, BelyiMaps Layer 9). Its continuations along paths in ℂ∖{0,1} are the finitely many conjugate functions on Y(H), so its minimal operator over ℚ̄(λ) has a full meromorphic local basis, in the sense of ConformalMappingPartII:O0/meromorphic-basis-monodromy, at every point of ℂ∖{0,1}.

Pull back along u↦16u^N. Because every cusp width of H divides 2N, a local coordinate at each cusp above λ=0 is a positive power of u, so the pulled-back operator also has a full meromorphic local basis at u=0. Its remaining finite singularities lie in 16^{−1/N}μ_N, outside U_N.

Multiply f by an integer clearing its common denominator and by a power of p clearing its pole at ∞. The product has χ-pullback in ℤ[[t]], so it lies in H(U_N,χ,ℤ). The multipliers lie in ℚ(p)^×, so the ℚ(λ)-span R₂N lies in W(U_N,χ,p).
acceptance: Do not infer trivial monodromy of an entire operator from one single-valued solution.
p(χ(t))=x(t^N) is integral; χ itself need not be (for N=3, χ=t−(8/3)t⁴+⋯).
The containment is stated for W. The printed bound for V over ℚ(p) fails for nonintegral χ (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendencePartII/E1), so the rank argument runs on W.

sources.locator: Proof of Proposition 3.0.1, pp.650–651; Definition 2.0.4, pp.635–636
sources.match: The proof places a basis of R₂N in the arithmetic holonomic ring for the λ-root coordinate and then bounds the larger span V. The target records the containment in the ℚ(λ)-span W, to which the corrected rank theorem applies; see E24.

nodes.title: Finiteness of the bounded-denominator field
nodes.statement: For each N≥1, R₂N is finite-dimensional over ℚ(λ). For N≥2 this follows from a holomorphic map φ, defined near the closed unit disc with image in U_N, φ(0)=0 and |φ′(0)|>1. Since R₂⊆R₄ under t↦t², the case N=1 follows from N=2; U₁=ℂ∖{1/16} is not hyperbolic and is not treated by a universal covering.
proofSteps: Fix N≥2 and the normalized covering F_N of ℂ∖μ_N (ConformalMappingPartII:U0/roots-cover). By ConformalMappingPartII:R0/positive-radius-expansion |F_N′(0)|=γ_N>16^{1/N}. Choose r<1 with rγ_N16^{−1/N}>1 and set φ(z)=16^{−1/N}F_N(rz).
Apply DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendencePartII:AA.4/rank-bound with p(u)=u^N and χ=x_N: W(U_N,χ,p) is finite-dimensional over ℚ(p)=ℚ(λ), and it contains R₂N by W3/holonomy-embedding.

For N=1 use R₂⊆R₄. The λ-root disc map u=x_N(t) has derivative one at 0 and is not a covering, so the Schwarz equality case (ConformalMappingPartII:U0/radius-schwarz) also gives the strict inequality without the explicit radius.
acceptance: Finiteness is proved before selecting a finite basis of R₂N.
The strict inequality |F_N′(0)|>16^{1/N} is needed; a disc map with derivative exactly one does not suffice.

sources.match: The field lemma uses a uniformization radius greater than one to obtain finite rank from the arithmetic holonomy bound. The target orders this before any finite-basis construction and treats the smallest level separately.

nodes.title: The two spans are fields
nodes.statement: M₂N and R₂N are finite-dimensional ℚ(λ)-subalgebras of the domain ℚ((t)); thus each is a field, with the inclusions ℚ(λ)→M₂N→R₂N injective.
proofSteps: Products of admissible generators have the common denominator product and the intersection group with the same level bound.
Multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space, hence surjective; solve for its inverse.
acceptance: The constant field is still ℚ; field structure does not add √2.

sources.match: The two spans are algebras inside a Laurent-series field. Finite-dimensionality then turns multiplication by a nonzero element into an invertible linear map, producing field inverses.

nodes.title: A normal stabilizer at exact geometric level
nodes.statement: There is a normal finite-index subgroup G₂N of SL₂(ℤ) with E≤G₂N≤⟨E,Γ(2N)⟩, L(G₂N)=2N, and every function of R₂N invariant under G₂N. For N=1 the upper group is Γ(2), whose signed level is 2.
proofSteps: Choose finitely many weak modular function generators spanning R₂N. Intersect their stabilizers AND ⟨E,Γ(2N)⟩ before taking the ambient normal core.
Each initial group has level dividing 2N and the included principal group forces the reverse level divisibility. All rational combinations remain invariant.
acceptance: For R₂=M₂ a basis {1} alone must not produce the full SL₂(ℤ) stabilizer.

sources.locator: Lemma 4.2.3, pp.655–656, with extraction correction E7
sources.match: The field lemma selects finitely many modular generators and takes a normal core. Adding the signed principal subgroup before taking the core repairs the unsupported exact-level claim.

nodes.title: The modular holonomy rank bound
nodes.statement: Let F_N:𝔻→ℂ∖μ_N be the normalized coverings of ConformalMappingPartII:U0/roots-cover. Suppose that for all sufficiently large N, |F_N′(0)|≥16^{1/N}(1+A/N³) for some A>0, and that for each fixed B>0 their circle means at r=1−B/N³ satisfy ∫log⁺|F_N(re^{iθ})|dθ/(2π)≤C_B(log N)/N. Then [R₂N:ℚ(λ)]≤C N³ log(2N) for all N≥1, after enlarging C for finitely many small levels.
proofSteps: Set φ(z)=16^{−1/N}F_N(rz) with r=1−A/(2N³). For N large, log|φ′(0)|≥log(1+A/N³)+log r≥cN⁻³ with c=A/3.

Use p(u)=u^N, so p∘χ=x(t^N) is integral. DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendencePartII:AA.4/rank-bound bounds dim_{ℚ(p)}W(U_N,χ,p) by e·∫log⁺|p∘φ|/log|φ′(0)|. Since log⁺|F^N/16|≤N log⁺|F|, the hypothesis with B=A/2 makes the numerator O(log N), so the bound is O(N³log N); R₂N⊆W by W3/holonomy-embedding.
Absorb all small N into C using W3/finite-rank; log(2N) avoids the zero bound that log N would give at N=1.
acceptance: All constants in the final bound are independent of N.
The mean estimate, not a supremum estimate exponential in N, is essential.

sources.match: The proposition combines a covering derivative gain of order N to the minus third power with a logarithmic boundary mean estimate. The target isolates those two inputs and obtains the uniform cubic-logarithmic field bound.

nodes.title: Nonabelian Ihara surjectivity
nodes.statement: Let N≥3, let E≤G≤⟨E,Γ(N)⟩ with G normal of finite index in SL₂(ℤ) and L(G)=N, and let p∤N be prime. Put S=⟨E,Γ(N)⟩/G, A=diag(p,1), D±=⟨E,Γ(N)⟩∩Γ₀(p) and D=Γ(N)∩Γ₀(p). The map D±→S×S, g↦(gG,AgA⁻¹G), is surjective, and so is its restriction to D. For g∈D± the conjugate AgA⁻¹ lies in ⟨E,Γ(N)⟩ and has upper-right entry divisible by p; conjugation by A does not preserve Γ₀(p).
proofSteps: Since E≤G, S≅Γ(N)/(G∩Γ(N)), so it suffices to treat the unsigned domain D=Γ(N)∩A⁻¹Γ(N)A. If the image were proper, Goursat (mathlib:Subgroup.goursat_surjective) would give a nontrivial common quotient Δ of S and maps g₁:Γ(N)→Δ, g₂:A⁻¹Γ(N)A→Δ agreeing on D.

By ModularCurvesPartII:R14.4/modular-amalgam (N≥3, p∤N), Γ_N(ℤ[1/p]) is the amalgam of Γ(N) and A⁻¹Γ(N)A over D, so g₁ and g₂ extend to one homomorphism Γ_N(ℤ[1/p])→Δ. By ModularCurvesPartII:R14.4/congruence-subgroup-property its kernel contains the principal congruence kernel of some level m prime to p, so K=ker(Γ(N)→Δ) is a congruence subgroup containing G∩Γ(N).
⟨E,K⟩ is congruence and contains E and G, so its signed level divides L(G)=N. W1/wohlfahrt gives Γ(N)≤⟨E,K⟩; since −I∉Γ(N) for N≥3, Γ(N)≤K, so Δ is trivial, a contradiction.
acceptance: If S is trivial, the result is the unique map onto the one-point product.
For N≤2 the cited amalgam is not asserted; the leveraging argument uses only levels 2N≥4.

sources.match: The nonabelian lemma uses Goursat, an arithmetic amalgam and the congruence subgroup property of SL₂(ℤ[1/p]) to rule out a common quotient. The target works on the unsigned domain, where the amalgam of ModularCurvesPartII applies, and corrects the codomain of conjugation by diag(p,1) (E17).

nodes.title: Triple surjectivity with the correct kernel
nodes.statement: Under the preceding hypotheses with N≥3, let D=Γ(N)∩Γ₀(p), and let B be the upper triangular subgroup of SL₂(𝔽p). The map D→S×S×B given by the two quotient maps and reduction modulo p is surjective. On this unsigned domain the reduction kernel is Γ(Np).
proofSteps: Because E⊆G, restricting from the signed to the unsigned domain leaves the S×S image unchanged (W4/nonabelian-ihara). The level-N unipotent [[1,N],[0,1]] lies in both quotient kernels and reduces onto the unipotent radical U of B.

Any proper image then comes, by Goursat, from a common quotient of S×S and the torus B/U, hence from a prime-order character. Restricted to Γ(N)∩Γ₁(p) it gives a pair of characters of S in the kernel of the enhanced Ihara map, which are congruence classes by ModularCurvesPartII:R14.4/enhanced-ihara.

A congruence class factoring through S has kernel containing G∩Γ(N) and some Γ(M); the signed closure of that kernel is congruence of level dividing N, so W1/wohlfahrt and N≥3 force the character to vanish. Reduction modulo p on Γ(N)∩Γ₀(p) has kernel Γ(Np) by CRT; E is adjoined only after this computation.
acceptance: −I is not silently identified with I modulo Np.

sources.match: The triple map adds the diagonal reduction character to the two noncongruence quotients. The target computes its reduction kernel on the unsigned principal-level domain before restoring the signs.

nodes.title: The group generation identity
nodes.statement: With N≥3 and the same G,p,A, the subgroup generated by E, G∩Γ(Np), and A⁻¹GA∩Γ₀(p) equals ⟨E,Γ(N)⟩∩Γ₀(p).
proofSteps: In the triple product, the images of ker(f₁,π) and ker(f₂) generate the product and both contain the full triple kernel. Their preimages therefore generate D.
On D these two kernels are G∩Γ(Np) and A⁻¹GA∩D. Adjoin E to recover the signed domain.
acceptance: This formulation remains correct when the signed reduction kernel is larger than Γ(Np).

sources.match: The generation formula follows by comparing images and kernels in the triple-surjectivity map. Its two generating subgroups and its intersection with Gamma-zero are retained exactly.

nodes.title: Geometric intersection and degree-preserving base change
nodes.statement: For p∤2N, R₂N∩M₂Np=M₂N and [R₂N M₂Np:M₂Np]=[R₂N:M₂N], with every field embedded by the stated q parameter. The second equality is a linear-disjointness assertion; it is not a formal consequence of the intersection for arbitrary extensions.
proofSteps: Intersection: an f in R₂N∩M₂Np is invariant under G₂N (W3/normal-stabilizer) and under Γ(2Np), so its stabilizer is a congruence subgroup containing E of signed level dividing 2N, and W1/wohlfahrt gives invariance under Γ(2N). By the rational-cusp model (MODEL) the rational-coefficient functions on X(2N) are exactly M₂N.

Complex scalars change no degree: ℚ((t)) and ℂ are linearly disjoint over ℚ inside ℂ((t)) (compare coefficients), so for finite extensions K⊆L of subfields of ℚ((t)), L⊗_K ℂK is a field mapping isomorphically onto ℂL and [ℂL:ℂK]=[L:K].

Over ℂ, MODEL identifies ℂM₂m with the function field of X(m). ℂM₂Np is Galois over ℂM₂N, with group a quotient of ⟨E,Γ(2N)⟩/⟨E,Γ(2Np)⟩, and ℂR₂N∩ℂM₂Np=ℂM₂N by the argument of the first step. A Galois extension is linearly disjoint from any extension meeting it only in the base, which gives the degree identity over ℂ and hence over ℚ.
acceptance: A field-intersection equality without the Galois linear-disjointness step is insufficient.
The descent from ℂ to ℚ is formal; the only modular input is the rational ∞-cusp model.

sources.locator: Proof of Theorem 4.3.2, pp.656–657; model statement in Lemma 4.2.3, p.656
sources.match: The degree proof uses a congruence intersection statement together with geometric base change over rational cusp models. The target separates these assertions because intersection alone does not imply linear disjointness.

nodes.title: p-scaling separates a noncongruence function
nodes.statement: For N≥1 and p∤2N, if a weight-zero function f∈R₂N is not invariant under any congruence subgroup, then f(pτ) is not in the M₂Np-algebra generated by R₂N. Consequently f(pτ)∈R₂Np supplies a genuinely new field element.
proofSteps: Any polynomial or rational expression in the compositum of R₂N and M₂Np is fixed by Γ(2Np)∩G₂N. The assumed expression for f(pτ) is also fixed by A⁻¹G₂NA∩SL₂(ℤ), whose level divides 2Np by W1/level-scaling.

Apply W4/generation at the level 2N≥4; if the starting level is 2, first pass to 4, which keeps f noncongruence since R₂⊆R₄ and M₂p⊆M₄p. The two groups generate ⟨E,Γ(2N)⟩∩Γ₀(p); unwinding the conjugation shows that f is invariant under a congruence subgroup, a contradiction.
acceptance: The initial f belongs to R₂N, correcting the inconsistent level in the printed degree proof.

sources.match: The leveraging theorem says that p-scaling a noncongruence modular function creates an element outside the old-level compositum. The corrected generation formula is the group-theoretic obstruction to such an expression.

nodes.title: Degree doubling
nodes.statement: If [R₂N:M₂N]>1 and p∤2N is prime, then [R₂Np:M₂Np]≥2[R₂N:M₂N].
proofSteps: Choose a generating weak modular function in R₂N outside M₂N and clear its common denominator and its pole at ∞. By Wohlfahrt it cannot be a congruence function at another level.
Its p-scaling lies outside the compositum, so the extension above that compositum has degree at least two. Use the degree-preserving base-change identity and the tower law.
acceptance: The chosen generator is at the old level; the new field is produced by scaling.

sources.match: The degree theorem combines separation of the scaled function with degree-preserving base change. The counterexample is chosen at the old level, correcting an inconsistent field label in the proof.

nodes.title: The congruence degree comparison
nodes.statement: For N>1, [M₂N:ℚ(λ)]=(2N)³/12·∏_{p∣2N}(1−p⁻²)>4N³/π². For N=1 the degree is 1. The formula uses the projective index: −I∈Γ(2) and −I∉Γ(2N) for N>1.
proofSteps: By MODEL, ℂM₂N is the function field of X(2N); so [M₂N:ℚ(λ)] is the degree of X(2N)→X(2), which is the projective index [Γ(2):±Γ(2N)] (FuchsianOrbifolds Layer 5, W2/lambda-covering). Linear disjointness of ℚ((t)) and ℂ over ℚ transfers the degree to ℚ.
Count SL₂(ℤ/m) by prime-power reduction and CRT, then divide the Γ(2)-relative index by two since −I∈Γ(2) and −I∉Γ(2N) for N>1.
Bound the finite Euler product below by 1/ζ(2)=6/π².
acceptance: N=2 yields degree 4; substituting N=1 into the generic formula would incorrectly yield 1/2.

sources.match: The index formula supplies the cubic lower bound for the congruence field. The target uses the projective index and separates N=1, where the displayed generic formula does not apply.

nodes.title: Leveraging contradicts logarithmic normalized degree
nodes.statement: If [R₂N:ℚ(λ)]≤C N³ log(2N) for a constant C and all N≥1, then R₂N=M₂N for every N.
proofSteps: A counterexample at N yields normalized degree at least 2 to the number of primes ≤X not dividing 2N, by repeated doubling.
Chebyshev’s lower bound gives at least cX/log X such primes eventually, while the upper bound gives log of their product O(X). The hypothesized normalized degree is O(X).
Taking logarithms contradicts cX/log X≤O(log X). The prime number theorem used in the source is stronger than necessary.
acceptance: Uniformity of C in N is essential.

sources.match: The proposition iterates degree doubling along primes until it exceeds the cubic-logarithmic bound after normalization. The target uses the pinned Chebyshev estimates, which suffice in place of the stronger prime number theorem.

nodes.title: Equality of the bounded and congruence fields
nodes.statement: For every N≥1 the embedded fields R₂N and M₂N coincide.
proofSteps: ConformalMappingPartII:R0/positive-radius-expansion gives |F_N′(0)|=γ_N≥16^{1/N}(1+ζ(3)/(2N³)) for every N≥2, which is the first hypothesis of W3/quantitative-rank with A=ζ(3)/2.
ConformalMappingPartII:M0/uniform-mean-growth with p(x)=x^N and r=1−B/N³ bounds ∫log⁺|F_N^N| by C log(N⁴/B). Dividing by N gives the second hypothesis, with C_B depending only on B.
W3/quantitative-rank then gives [R₂N:ℚ(λ)]≤CN³log(2N) for all N, and W5/leveraging-contradiction gives R₂N=M₂N.
acceptance: The conclusion is equality in the chosen rational Laurent field, not merely an abstract field isomorphism.

sources.locator: §6.3, pp.685–686, assembling Proposition 3.0.1 with Theorems 5.1.4 and 6.0.1
sources.match: The final proof combines the analytic rank bound with leveraging to identify the bounded-denominator and congruence fields at every level.

nodes.title: Integral reduction to weight zero
nodes.statement: Let h₀(τ)=λ(τ)/(16η(τ/2)²). It is holomorphic and nonzero on ℍ, has weight −1 on a congruence subgroup, and its normalized expansion is q^(11/12) times an integral unit with constant term 1. Its inverse has the same integral-unit property after the opposite monomial shift. Thus for any integer k, f↦f h₀^k changes weight k to weight zero on a finite-index group and preserves bounded denominators after enlarging the strict period. A power of λ can clear the remaining pole at ∞.
proofSteps: Compute the η products with the q=e^{πiτ} convention; use the theta/eta multiplier supplier to find a congruence character kernel.
Integral products and their unit inverses preserve the arithmetic condition. The multiplier is killed by restriction to a congruence subgroup, with period enlarged to include 12.
acceptance: Negative k requires the inverse unit, not just the forward product.

sources.match: The introductory reduction uses a fixed eta-lambda weight-minus-one form with integral unit expansion after a monomial shift. The target includes the inverse needed for negative weights and a common finite congruence kernel.

nodes.title: The unbounded denominators theorem
nodes.statement: Let N≥1, k∈ℤ and Γ≤SL₂(ℤ) have finite index. If f is a weight-k weak form on Γ, holomorphic at ∞ with strict period 2N, and every coefficient of its actual q^{1/N} expansion is in ℤ, then there exists a congruence subgroup Γ′ on which f is a weight-k weak form. Poles at other cusps are allowed.
proofSteps: Reduce to weight zero and enlarge the level to the lcm of all signed cusp widths, including the strict period and the multiplier kernel.
The transformed rational integral germ lies in R₂M=M₂M. It is a congruence modular function. Divide by the nonzero congruence factor and undo the principal-part shift.

nodes.title: Rational bounded denominators force congruence
nodes.statement: A rational Fourier expansion of a weak modular form, with one common denominator and a finite principal part, belongs to a congruence weak form. Equivalently a rational-coefficient weak form that is not invariant under any congruence subgroup has unbounded denominators at every cusp where its expansion is rational.
proofSteps: Clear cusp poles by Δ and the single scalar denominator, apply the integral theorem, and divide by Δ.
Move another rational cusp to ∞ using the slash action; retain its strict translation width.
acceptance: A noncongruence subgroup can carry congruence forms; the hypothesis concerns the form itself.

nodes.title: Algebraic-integer Fourier coefficients
nodes.statement: If a weak modular form of integer weight has an expansion at ∞ in O_K[[q^{1/N}]] for a number field K⊆ℂ, then it is a congruence weak form. The same conclusion holds for an expansion in the algebraic integers Q̄ with the common-number-field and conjugation bridge NF supplied. One scalar denominator over O_K and finitely many negative exponents are also allowed.
proofSteps: After reducing weight and making the algebraic modular-function model explicit, realize coefficientwise conjugates as weak modular functions on finite-index groups.

For an integral basis α_i of O_K, take coefficientwise Tr(α_i f); these have integral rational expansions and are weak on intersections of finitely many conjugate groups. Apply the rational theorem and invert the nondegenerate trace matrix.
For Q̄ coefficients first prove the single-number-field assertion in NF; it is not a property of arbitrary algebraic-integer power series.

nodes.title: The integral cube root of j
nodes.statement: In the standard parameter Q=e^{2πiτ}, the branch j^(1/3)=E₄/η⁸=Q^(−1/3)(1+248Q+4124Q²+34752Q³+⋯) has integral Laurent coefficients and is a weak modular function on a level-3 congruence subgroup. Multiplying it by Δ brings it within the holomorphic-at-∞ hypothesis of W6.
proofSteps: Use the parent j identity j=E₄³/Δ and the integral product η⁻⁸. Fix the branch by its leading term.
Apply the main theorem after clearing the cusp pole, and verify the level-3 character directly from the η multiplier.

nodes.title: The h-root denominator test
nodes.statement: Set h=λ(1−λ)/16=q∏_{n≥1}((1+q^{2n})/(1+q^n))^{24}=q∏_{m odd}(1+q^m)^{−24}. It is a nowhere-vanishing weak modular function for the theta group ⟨Γ(2),S⟩, the conjugate of Γ₀(2) containing S. For n≥1, the branch h^{1/n} with leading term q^{1/n} has bounded denominators if and only if n∣24, and is a congruence weak modular function if and only if n∣24.
proofSteps: Write h=q·u with u=∏_{m odd}(1+q^m)^{−24}∈1+qℤ[[q]], using λ=(θ₂/θ₃)⁴, 1−λ=(θ₄/θ₃)⁴ and the theta product identities. If n∣24 every factor of u^{1/n} has integral exponent, so h^{1/n}=q^{1/n}u^{1/n} has integral coefficients.

Conversely let u^{1/n} have bounded denominators, let ℓ be prime and let c be minimal with ℓ^c u^{1/n}∈ℤ_(ℓ)[[q]]. If c≥1, the reduction of ℓ^c u^{1/n} modulo ℓ is nonzero while its n-th power ℓ^{cn}u reduces to 0, impossible in the domain 𝔽_ℓ[[q]]. So u^{1/n} is integral, and its q-coefficient −24/n is an integer.

S maps λ to 1−λ, so h is invariant under ⟨Γ(2),S⟩; it has no zeros on ℍ, so h^{1/n} is a weak modular function on the kernel of the induced character to ℤ/n. Bounded denominators give congruence by W6/rational-contrapositive, and congruence gives bounded denominators by the congruence bounded-denominator theorem.
acceptance: n=24 is integral after its monomial shift, while n=5 is not bounded: the coefficients of u^{1/5} have denominators 5, 25, 125, ….
With q=e^{πiτ}, T sends q to −q and h is not T-invariant; the invariance group is ⟨Γ(2),S⟩, not Γ₀(2) itself (E22).

nodes.title: The Fermat-cover test
nodes.statement: The cover u^n+v^n=1 above λ=u^n, for n≥1, is congruence precisely for n∈{1,2,4,8}. Its normalized branch (1−16x)^(1/n), x=λ/16, has bounded denominators precisely for those n.
proofSteps: For p odd dividing n, the p-adic valuations of the binomial coefficients go to −∞. If n=2^a, valuations after the factor 16^m are (4−a)m−v₂(m!) when a>0, so boundedness holds exactly for a≤3; handle n=1 directly.

The branch u=λ^(1/n) is an integral unit after its monomial shift for n=1,2,4,8; prove this by the λ product or a theta/eta identity. The two branches then give congruence by W6, and the converse follows from the imported congruence denominator theorem.
acceptance: n=8 passes and n=16 fails. Odd n>1 fails at an odd prime divisor.

sources.match: The Fermat example gives exactly exponents one, two, four and eight. The target uses the binomial valuation obstruction and checks the second cover coordinate, not just one radical.

nodes.title: Algebraicity for integral three-point ODE solutions
nodes.statement: Let f∈ℤ[[x]] solve a nonzero linear differential operator over ℚ̄(x), with no genuine singularities outside {0,1/16,∞}, and with finite local monodromy at 0 in the supplier’s meromorphic-after-finite-ramification sense. Apparent singularities are allowed only when every local solution is meromorphic. Then f is algebraic over ℚ(x). In the regular-singular case the stated finite-monodromy condition is the usual finite-order local monodromy condition.
proofSteps: Let N be the order of the local monodromy at 0, replaced by 2N if N=1, so that N≥2. The pullback g(u)=f(u^N) is integral and is annihilated by the pulled-back operator. That operator has a full meromorphic local basis at u=0 and at every apparent singularity, in the sense of ConformalMappingPartII:O0/meromorphic-basis-monodromy; its genuine finite singularities lie in 16^{−1/N}μ_N. So g∈H(U_N,t,ℤ) (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendencePartII:AA.4/holonomic-ring).

Take φ(z)=16^{−1/N}F_N(rz) with |φ′(0)|>1, using ConformalMappingPartII:R0/positive-radius-expansion. All powers g^k lie in the ring H (AA.4/holonomic-closure), so they span a subspace of W(U_N,t,u) of finite dimension over ℚ(u) by AA.4/rank-bound.
Hence g is algebraic over ℚ(u), and f(x)=g(x^{1/N}) is algebraic over ℚ(x). The meromorphic-basis convention matters: bare single-valuedness does not exclude an essential singularity.
acceptance: The Jacobi K₀ series is integral and transcendental; its entire local solution space has infinite unipotent monodromy at 0.

sources.locator: Theorem 7.2.1 and footnote 4, pp.687–688; Definition 2.0.4 convention, p.635

nodes.title: The congruence refinement for ODE solutions
nodes.statement: Under W7/ode-algebraicity, the distinguished continuation f(λ(τ)/16) is invariant under Γ(M) for some M≥1. If the scalar solution has apparent poles on ℍ, it is a meromorphic congruence modular function; if it has none, it is weakly holomorphic.
proofSteps: The algebraic germ has finitely many branches and gives a finite-index stabilizer under the Γ(2) covering.
Multiply by an integral polynomial in λ clearing apparent interior poles and a monomial clearing the cusp principal part. Its Fourier expansion remains integral; apply W6 and divide back.
acceptance: Do not silently call a function with an apparent interior pole a weak form.

nodes.title: Vector-valued modular forms
nodes.statement: For n≥0, k∈ℤ, a vector-valued form consists of ρ:PSL₂(ℤ)→GL_n(ℂ) and a holomorphic F:ℍ→ℂⁿ with F|ₖγ=ρ(γ)F after pullback to SL₂(ℤ), semisimple ρ(T), and the following growth: for every real a<b and C>0 there are A,B>0 such that each |F_j(τ)|≤A exp(B Im τ) when a≤Re τ≤b and Im τ≥C. Since ρ(−I)=1, nonzero such forms have even weight. The SL₂ version with central character is a separate imported parity convention.
proofSteps: Use the pinned finite-dimensional complex vector spaces, general linear group and componentwise holomorphy/slash action.
State exponential growth on every vertical strip and retain semisimplicity as an actual hypothesis, not a conclusion of growth.
acceptance: Dimension zero and the zero vector are allowed; no spanning assumption is hidden in the definition.

nodes.title: Generalized Fourier expansions without logarithms
nodes.statement: In a basis diagonalizing ρ(T), each component has a convergent expansion Q^μ Σ_{m≥m₀}a_m Q^m, Q=e^{2πiτ}, where exp(2πiμ) is its T-eigenvalue and μ may be complex. Conversely such expansions with finite lower support give the required moderate exponential strip growth. There are no logarithms; rational exponents or finite-order T are not asserted.
proofSteps: Twist an eigencomponent by exp(−2πiμτ) to make it 1-periodic. Descend to a punctured disc and use the exponential growth to bound its pole order.
Recover growth from the finite principal part and a convergent holomorphic remainder.

For groups excluding E or odd weight use the parent SL₂ central-character convention.

Finite-order permutation T is semisimple over ℂ.

Build it by descent of the trivial bundle on ℍ with its flat connection. It has this specified rank independently of linear relations between component functions. This does not define an integral free module or an arithmetic connection.

nodes.title: The minimal operator of a component germ
nodes.statement: With x=λ/16, the continuation space W_j of a weight-zero component f=F_j is the full solution space, at an ordinary point, of a unique monic operator L_j∈ℂ(x)[∂] of order dim W_j. L_j is the minimal operator of the germ f. It is regular singular, has no genuine singularities outside {0,1/16,∞}, and has apparent singularities only at points of ℍ where all its local solutions are holomorphic. Its local monodromies are those of W_j, hence semisimple.
proofSteps: Choose a basis w₁,…,w_m of W_j and set L_j(y)=Wr(y,w₁,…,w_m)/Wr(w₁,…,w_m), with Wronskians in x. Continuation multiplies both Wronskians by the same determinant, so the coefficients of L_j are single-valued on Y(2). They are meromorphic on ℍ because x is a local coordinate there (W2/lambda-covering).

Each w_i is a constant combination of the components of F, which have moderate growth at the cusps (W7/generalized-expansion). So the coefficients have moderate growth at the three cusps, extend meromorphically to X(2)≅ℙ¹ and lie in ℂ(x). Moderate growth of all solutions gives regular singularities by Fuchs' criterion.

Every operator annihilating f annihilates all its continuations, so L_j right-divides it; L_j is the minimal operator of f. Zeros of the Wronskian on ℍ are apparent singularities with holomorphic local solutions. Local monodromy on W_j is the action of the semisimple cusp monodromy on an invariant subquotient (W7/component-continuation).
acceptance: An abstract Riemann–Hilbert existence statement without the actual scalar germ is insufficient.
For f=1 the operator is ∂, of order one.

sources.match: The component proof needs a differential equation for the selected scalar germ with regular singularities and the local monodromy of the component. The target constructs it from the continuation space by Wronskians instead of the rank-6n bundle of the printed proof (E13).

nodes.title: Arithmetic descent and finite component monodromy
nodes.statement: If the selected weight-zero component has an integral x-series f∈ℤ[[x]], then its minimal operator L_j has coefficients in ℚ(x), f is a G-function, the companion system of L_j satisfies Galochkin's condition, L_j is globally nilpotent and its local monodromies are quasi-unipotent. Together with semisimplicity, every local monodromy of W_j has finite order.
proofSteps: For σ∈Aut(ℂ/ℚ), applying σ to the coefficients of L_j gives a monic operator of the same order that still annihilates the formal series f, whose coefficients are rational. By minimality it equals L_j, so the coefficients of L_j are fixed by Aut(ℂ/ℚ) and lie in ℚ(x).

f converges near 0, since its q-expansion converges on the unit disc and x is a local coordinate at the cusp, and its coefficients are integers; with the equation of the previous step it is a G-function (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.5/g-function), and so are its derivatives. By minimality f,f′,…,f^{(m−1)} are linearly independent over ℚ̄(x) and solve the companion system, which therefore satisfies Galochkin's condition (DT.5/chudnovsky-galochkin-condition).

Galochkin's condition implies global nilpotence (Bombieri–André), and a globally nilpotent operator has quasi-unipotent local monodromy at every point (Katz). These two theorems are the request GLOCAL. Quasi-unipotent and semisimple local monodromy has finite order.
acceptance: A theorem for a ℚ̄(x)-linearly independent vector of G-functions is applied to the companion system of the minimal operator of f, not to an unspecified ambient system.
The descent to ℚ(x) uses only that f has rational coefficients; no arithmetic model of the representation is needed.

sources.match: The proof applies the Chudnovsky, Bombieri–André and Katz theorems to obtain quasi-unipotent and hence finite local monodromy. The target applies them to the minimal operator of the selected integral series, after proving that operator is defined over ℚ(x).

nodes.title: Arithmetic normalization of a vector-valued component
nodes.statement: For a nonzero even-weight vector-valued form of weight k, choose an integral scalar congruence form g of weight k′≥0 with 12∣k+k′. Multiply F by g·(λ/(16Δ(τ/2)))^((k+k′)/12), choosing the branch with leading term 1. This has weight zero after restriction to a finite congruence cover, preserves an integral selected Fourier germ, and has only finite-order additional monodromy. Division back recovers congruence of the original selected component.
proofSteps: Choose k′ from weights 4 and 6 with the needed congruence; negative k is allowed by taking k′ large. The ratio λ/(16Δ(τ/2)) is an integral unit with constant term 1.

Validate the multiplier and weight −12 of the ratio; the exponent is integral. Restrict to a common congruence kernel. Zeros of g are permitted: at the end use the known holomorphy of the original quotient.
acceptance: The normalization starts with 1 in q; a mistaken Δ argument introduces a fractional leading monomial.

Use the three-point ODE congruence theorem, then undo the scalar congruence factor. Zero components are immediate.

nodes.title: Mason’s corollary on the effective value span
nodes.statement: Suppose each component of F becomes an integral Fourier series after multiplication by a nonzero scalar and enlargement of its strict period. Put V_F=span_ℂ{F(τ):τ∈ℍ}. Then V_F is ρ-stable and Γ(M) acts identically on V_F for some M. If V_F=ℂⁿ, ker ρ contains Γ(M) and ρ has finite image. Without spanning, the conclusion applies only to ρ|V_F.
proofSteps: If a component F_j has, after a scalar, an integral expansion in Q^{1/M}, replace τ by Mτ: τ↦F(Mτ) is a vector-valued form for the finite-index group SL₂(ℤ)∩diag(M,1)⁻¹SL₂(ℤ)diag(M,1), and inducing it to SL₂(ℤ) keeps T semisimple and the strip growth. Its component F_j(Mτ) has an integral expansion in Q, so the component theorem applies, and congruence of F_j(Mτ) gives congruence of F_j.
Intersect the finitely many congruence groups. The vector slash law then fixes every value F(τ), hence its span.
Finite index gives finite image only for the representation restricted to that span.

nodes.statement: Set σ(S)=diag(1,−1), σ(R)=[[2,1],[−7,−3]] for the presentation PSL₂(ℤ)=⟨S,R:S²=R³=1⟩, and T=SR. Then σ(T)=[[2,1],[7,3]] is semisimple of infinite order. The pair ρ=1⊕σ, F=(1,0,0), k=0 satisfies the vector-valued definition with integral coefficients but ρ has infinite image.

The constant first coordinate transforms trivially and the others vanish, so the strip growth and slash identity hold.

nodes.title: Positive-weight forms and infinite monodromy
nodes.statement: Let h be a nonzero congruence form of positive integer weight k, modular on Γ′, and express it as a germ in x=λ/16 on the finite étale cover Y(Γ′∩Γ(2))→Y(2). Its continuation space is spanned by τ^i h for 0≤i≤k, so its minimal operator has order exactly k+1. The monodromy on this space is Sym^k of the standard representation, has infinite image, and is unipotent and nontrivial at every cusp. Apparent singularities on ℍ occur exactly at the zeros of h. If h has an actual expansion in ℤ[[q]], integral inverse λ reparametrization gives an integral x-series; for a fractional q-expansion the corresponding Puiseux germ is retained, and integrality after a fractional change is not asserted without checking its unit root.
proofSteps: Continuing h along a loop that represents γ=[[a,b],[c,d]]∈Γ′ replaces it by (cτ+d)^k h. Since Γ′ is Zariski dense in SL₂, these span all of {P(τ)h : deg P≤k}, of dimension k+1; this is the continuation space, so the minimal operator has order k+1.

The Wronskian of h,τh,…,τ^k h in x is a nonzero constant times h^{k+1}(dτ/dx)^{k(k+1)/2}, and dτ/dx has no zeros or poles on ℍ. So the singular points of the operator on ℍ are the zeros of h, where all local solutions are holomorphic.
The monodromy acts on polynomials of degree at most k in τ through Sym^k of the standard representation of Γ′; parabolic elements act unipotently and nontrivially for k≥1, and the image is infinite.
acceptance: This is the positive-weight boundary example: its local monodromy at 0 is infinite, so the finite-monodromy ODE theorem does not apply.
For Δ (k=12) the operator has order 13 on Y(2), with apparent singularities only where Δ vanishes, which is nowhere on ℍ.

nodes.title: Weakly holomorphic quasimodular forms
nodes.statement: For a finite-index Γ≤SL₂(ℤ), use its integral-weight modular-form ring M(Γ) from the parent, retaining its central-character convention. If E≤Γ, only even weights contribute. Set M̃(Γ)=M(Γ)[E₂] and M̃!(Γ)=M̃(Γ)[Δ⁻¹] inside holomorphic functions on ℍ. Equivalently M̃!=M!(Γ)[E₂]. Weights and quasimodular depth are retained as filtrations. The existing E₂ is used; this is not a new definition of the Eisenstein series.
proofSteps: Embed the parent graded modular ring into functions, adjoin the pinned E₂, and localize at the nowhere-vanishing Δ.

nodes.title: Cuspidal arithmetic components and deficient places
nodes.statement: Fix a number field K⊆ℂ and a representation ρ. Let S_k(ρ;K) be the K-space of cuspidal vector-valued forms whose components have actual expansions in tK[[t]] for t=q^(1/N), some common N. A normalized place v of K is deficient if some such component Σ_{m≥1}a_m t^m has unbounded |a_m|_v at a finite v, or unbounded |a_m|_v/m^((k−1)/2+ε) for some ε>0 at an archimedean v. An archimedean place uses its usual modulus, not its square. The source's version is K=ℚ; the number-field version specializes to it.
proofSteps: Quantify actual cuspidal arithmetic forms and their components before their coefficient-growth witnesses. Fix the expansion parameter and absolute-value normalization.
Use the cofinal parameter changes t↦t^r to show that changing the common denominator of exponents only changes growth constants.

nodes.title: A finite deficient place from an arithmetic witness
nodes.statement: Let a cuspidal component f over K be noncongruence. If its coefficient denominators are supported on a finite set S of finite places, then at least one v∈S is deficient. Thus an ambient representation conclusion additionally needs arithmetic forms detecting its noncongruence effective representation. These two hypotheses are not omitted.
proofSteps: If every v∈S were bounded, their finitely many bounds could be cleared by a single element of O_K. Places outside S are already integral, giving a global common denominator.

review.notes: Independent review by Claude (session claude-HAvIjQ) of Codex's DESIGN-ModularFormsPartII, 2026-10-19. Read CDT25 (published offprint, SHA-256 matching) pp.627–632, 649–666, 667–673 (statements), 685–697, KSV10 pp.4–6, the upstream READMEs at the pull-request heads of ModularCurvesPartII (#913), DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence (#855), AlgebraicModularFormsAndSerreWeights (#928), ArithmeticGaloisDuality (#858), ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations (#856), InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups (#850) and AutomorphicGaloisRepresentations (#1007), and the accepted atlas packets of ModularCurvesPartII, DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendencePartII and ConformalMappingPartII.
